Paris

(Thanks for news of home. Will be taking some introductions around today.)
#### Paris
(Thanks for clippings. Will be happy to get  $ \underline{\text{Outlook}} $ as present. For Xmas a necktie or something small, or might buy small guidebook of Paris as guide and memento of trip.)

I have just received in this morning's mail a copy of your paper on the 'Real Issue' between yourself and Professor Royce, -- sent on to me from Oakland by my father. In the dullness of the French provinces, remote from philosophical books and from English books of any sort, it is peculiarly refreshing and stimulating to get hold of so clear and vigorous a statement on the philosophical problems that one is interested in; and I therefore venture to write to thank you for printing it, and at the same time to ask for more of the same kind. I do this latter, more particularly, as the result of some observation of the direction of the currents of philosophical opinion among the students in the department at Harvard. There was last year--

among that part, at least, of the more advanced students whose philosophical interests had not been corrupted by the laboratory habit--a great deal of very free and lively discussion over the central metaphysical questions--both in private and in the semi-public conferences at Professor Royce's; and these discussions were pretty likely to find their starting point in some one or other of the arguments in the "Conception of God." Have been enjoying some reading of Guyau--a singularly fresh and vigorous and engaging mind, the most original of the younger Frenchmen and the most fruitful of the evolutionary philosophers. He was another of the consumptive geniuses,--died at 33, having written half a score of books, beginning with one at nineteen which was crowned by the French Academy. He is admirable for his intellectual intrepidity and honesty; the doctrine which he, in the desire to avoid any possible confusion of it with traditional views, calls the Irreligion of the Future would have been proclaimed by an Englishman, if he had been the author of it, to be identical with the creeds of the Anglican church. It is characteristic of our race,--and not a wholly undesirable quality--that it never enjoys its new wine unless it has it in old wine skins. Guyau's doctrines, of course, won't last, but he abounds in interesting apercus, and his philosophy has a permanent claim as the expression of an exceptionally large and vital personality.

I thought of my Pater last week in rereading a little Browning. Am glad to hear the lectures began so promisingly. With much love Yr. aff. son Arthur O.L.
